The eastern quoll (Dasyurus viverrinus) is a medium-sized dasyurid marsupial once widespread across southeastern Australia. Neonates emerge after a remarkably brief gestation period of 20 days [tg = 20 days], a value recorded in captive colonies maintained at a core body temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. At birth, the altricial young are minuscule, each weighing only 0.0235 grams [Wwb = 0.0235 grams], reflecting the extreme developmental immaturity typical of marsupial newborns. These tiny neonates then undertake an arduous climb to the mother's pouch, where they will attach to a teat and remain for a prolonged period of continuous suckling. The duration of this dependence is considerable, as the time since birth at weaning is 168 days since birth [tx = 168 days since birth] under stable maternal thermal conditions at a temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. At this point of weaning, a juvenile eastern quoll has reached a wet weight of approximately 600 grams [Wwx = approximately 600 grams], representing a massive increase from its birth size and signaling the onset of nutritional independence. This pattern of extremely altricial birth followed by an extended period of pouch life and lactation is consistent with the broader reproductive strategy exhibited across the genus Dasyurus, reflecting a common marsupial adaptation to limited maternal energy reserves during early development.

Adult body size in this species shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common trait among carnivorous marsupials. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 700 grams [Wwi = 700 grams], while males grow substantially larger, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 1100 grams [Wwi = 1100 grams]. This difference in mass is matched by a corresponding disparity in overall body length; the ultimate total length for females is 57 centimeters [Li = 57 centimeters], whereas males achieve a more imposing ultimate total length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters]. Field measurements from a study in Tasmania, where the species now persists in the wild, confirmed these dimorphic size ranges, which are thought to be driven by sexual selection for larger male body size in competition for access to females during the breeding season. The larger body size of males also likely confers advantages in securing territories and dominating food resources, although it imposes higher absolute metabolic costs that may contribute to a slightly different life history trajectory between the sexes.

The reproductive biology of the eastern quoll is tightly linked to the seasonal availability of resources, with breeding typically occurring in the austral winter. Under controlled captive conditions with a stable ambient temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C] reflecting the species' thermoneutral zone, female reproductive output is constrained by the number of teats available in the pouch. On average, a female reproductively active adult produces one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], and each litter contains up to 6 young [N_R_i = each litter contains up to 6 young]. This maximum reproductive rate, therefore, can be expressed as a single litter of 6 offspring born annually. The timing of this reproductive event is critical, as the young must be weaned and independent by the time resources become plentiful in the spring. The relatively small litter size, compared to some smaller dasyurids, is likely a reflection of the trade-off between offspring size and number, given the substantial 600 grams [Wwx = 600 grams] mass at which the young are weaned.

The species exhibits a relatively slow life history for a mammal of its size, with a maximum documented lifespan of 6.8 years [am = 6.8 years] recorded in a captive individual under thermoneutral conditions at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. This longevity is considerably longer than that of many smaller dasyurid species, which often exhibit semelparous or short-lived life cycles, and likely reflects the eastern quoll's larger body mass and more stable, aseasonal energy budget in captivity. The journey from birth to reproductive maturity is also a protracted affair. Females reach a state of sexual maturation relatively late, with the time since birth at puberty recorded as 335 days since birth [tp = 335 days since birth] under ideal captive thermal conditions at a temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. This delay before the onset of first oestrus and reproductive viability is a critical life history phase during which the juvenile must complete its somatic growth and establish a robust body condition sufficient to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.

The ecological role of the eastern quoll as a generalist predator and scavenger has been well documented in its last remaining stronghold of Tasmania. Body size dimorphism influences prey selection, with the larger males, possessing an ultimate total length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], capable of tackling larger vertebrate prey than the smaller females, whose ultimate total length of 57 centimeters [Li = 57 centimeters] restricts them to smaller mammals, birds, and insects. Males, at roughly 1.1 kilograms (1100 grams) [Wwi = 1100 grams], exhibit a body mass approximately 57% greater than that of females (700 grams) [Wwi = 700 grams], a degree of dimorphism that is among the highest recorded in the genus Dasyurus and may reflect distinct evolutionary pressures on each sex regarding territory defense and reproductive strategy. Although now extinct on the Australian mainland, the Tasmanian populations of Dasyurus viverrinus continue to be the subject of intensive research, with recent studies focusing on the impacts of disease, habitat fragmentation, and introduced predators on their demography and long-term viability in the wild.
